stories.headline: Myanmar rejects UN court's finding that it committed genocide against the Rohingya
stories.summary: The International Court of Justice ruled on Thursday that Myanmar committed genocide against the Rohingya Muslim minority, in a case brought by Gambia. Myanmar's military-backed government called the ruling "unfair", and rights groups urged governments to impose sanctions. The court ordered reparations, safe return for those who fled and prosecutions, but it has no way to enforce the ruling.
stories.why_it_matters: It is reported to be the first time the UN's top court has held a state responsible for genocide, and analysts quoted in the coverage say the way the court judged intent could shape other genocide cases, including the one against Israel. For Rohingya refugees, little changes soon, because the court cannot enforce its orders.
stories.background: The Rohingya are a mostly Muslim minority from Myanmar, many of whom fled to neighbouring Bangladesh to escape military violence and still live in refugee camps there. Gambia brought a case against Myanmar at the International Court of Justice in 2019 under the 1948 Genocide Convention, and the court ruled in 2022 that it had jurisdiction. The ICJ, based in The Hague, settles disputes between states; it does not try individuals. Its rulings are binding, but it has no enforcement arm, so a state that believes a ruling is being ignored can turn to the UN Security Council.

facts.text: The International Court of Justice ruled on Thursday, Nov. 19, that Myanmar committed genocide against the Rohingya.
The ruling orders Myanmar to let those who fled return home safely, to pay reparations to the Rohingya and to prosecute people suspected of genocide; the court has no power to enforce it.
The judges decided for Gambia by nine votes to six, and reports describe it as the first time the court has held a state responsible for genocide.
The amount of compensation is to be set in later proceedings, and the judgment does not order Myanmar to grant the Rohingya citizenship.
Myanmar dismissed the ruling as "unfair".
Rights groups urged governments to impose sanctions on Myanmar after the ruling.
Rohingya refugees in Bangladesh welcomed the verdict but told the AP they want to go home to Myanmar.

stories.headline: Russia hits Kyiv bridges in large attack as missiles come down in Poland
stories.summary: Russia struck bridges and railway stations in Kyiv in what President Volodymyr Zelenskyy called one of the largest aerial attacks of the war. During the attack, two Russian missiles and a suspected drone came down in Poland, which the Polish prime minister said was likely a deliberate provocation; NATO called it a grave violation of Polish airspace. On Saturday a missile strike on Kryvyi Rih killed two people and wounded about 60.
stories.why_it_matters: Missiles landing on the territory of a NATO member raise the risk that the war spreads beyond Ukraine, while the strikes on Kyiv's bridges and power supply hit the daily lives of millions of residents.
stories.background: Russia launched its full-scale invasion of Ukraine in 2022, and the war is now close to five years old. Earlier this week Ukraine damaged the bridge linking Russia to Crimea, the peninsula Russia annexed in 2014, and President Vladimir Putin vowed retaliation. Poland borders Ukraine and is a member of NATO, whose members treat an attack on one as an attack on all. Thousands of European troops from 11 countries were holding an exercise in southeastern Poland this week to prepare for a possible mission in Ukraine after the war. Separately, the US has raised discussing wider European security in talks with Russia, which the AP reports has worried Ukraine and its allies.

facts.text: Russian missiles hit bridges in Kyiv in an overnight attack; officials in the capital said three bridges were struck.
The BBC reported that railway stations in Kyiv were also hit, and ABC News reported that power was cut.
Zelenskyy said it was one of the largest aerial attacks since the invasion began.
The attack followed Putin's vow of retaliation after Ukraine damaged the Crimea bridge this week.
Poland's defence minister, Władysław Kosiniak-Kamysz, said two missiles and a drone from Russia violated Polish airspace overnight.
Poland's prime minister said the crash was likely an intentional provocation timed to European military exercises in Poland, and NATO called it a "grave violation" of Polish airspace.
There were no injuries or damage from the three incidents in Poland, according to The New York Times.
One missile crashed about 35 kilometres from an area linked to the exercises, France 24 reported.
A ballistic missile strike on Kryvyi Rih, Zelenskyy's hometown, killed two people and wounded 60 on Saturday.
Russia is reviving demands it made before the war after US envoys proposed discussing broader European security at Ukraine talks, the AP reported.

stories.headline: Houthis fire missiles at Riyadh after Saudi-led strikes on Yemen
stories.summary: The Saudi-led coalition said it intercepted three ballistic missiles fired toward Riyadh early Saturday by Yemen's Houthis, who had vowed reprisals for a coalition "special operation" in Yemen. Reuters reported that coalition forces struck a Yemeni port and that the Houthis warned airlines away from the kingdom. Separately, President Trump said Iran wants a deal but on terms he does not accept.
stories.why_it_matters: Renewed fighting between Saudi Arabia and the Houthis threatens civilians in both countries and air travel in the Gulf, and it comes as talks to end the war with Iran are stalled.
stories.background: The Houthis are an armed movement backed by Iran that controls much of Yemen, including the capital, Sanaa. A coalition led by Saudi Arabia has fought them on behalf of Yemen's internationally recognized government. Bloomberg reports that after four years of relative calm the war flared up again, and other outlets date the renewed fighting to this summer. The exchange comes during a wider conflict involving the United States and Iran, in which negotiations are under way but have not produced an agreement.

facts.text: The Saudi-led coalition said it intercepted and destroyed three ballistic missiles fired toward Riyadh early Saturday.
The Houthis said on X that they were striking targets across Saudi Arabia, including in Riyadh.
The missile fire followed Saudi-led coalition air raids on Yemen, after the Houthis vowed reprisals for what was described as a coalition "special operation".
Saudi-led forces struck a port in Yemen and the Houthis warned airlines to stay away from the kingdom, Reuters reported.
It was the second Houthi attack on the Saudi capital in recent days, France 24 reported.
Reuters reported that the Houthi attacks are adding to concerns about a US-Saudi nuclear power agreement.

Trump told reporters on Friday that Iran wants a deal but not one that is acceptable to him; Iran's foreign minister, Abbas Araqchi, said Tehran wants diplomacy and guarantees that Washington is serious about negotiating.

stories.headline: COP31 climate talks run into overtime with fossil fuels missing from draft deal
stories.summary: UN climate talks in Turkey ran past their Friday deadline as negotiators from nearly 200 countries remained split over fossil fuels and climate finance. A revised draft agreement makes no mention of phasing out fossil fuels, which drew criticism from activists and some leaders. Delegates put off some decisions until next year, and talks continued on Saturday.
stories.why_it_matters: The outcome shapes how quickly countries cut the coal, oil and gas use that drives more intense heat waves, droughts and floods, and how much money poorer countries get to cope with them.
stories.background: COP31 is this year's annual UN climate summit, a two-week meeting where nearly 200 countries negotiate a joint response to global warming. It is being held in Turkey, with Australia leading the negotiations. In 2023, at the summit in Dubai, countries agreed for the first time on language about moving away from fossil fuels, and how far to go beyond that has divided governments since. Decisions at these summits need consensus, so a small group of countries can block stronger wording.

facts.text: The talks went past their scheduled Friday end, and delegates deferred some decisions to next year.
The latest draft declaration does not mention a phaseout of fossil fuels.
An earlier draft had included an option calling for accelerated action to phase out fossil fuels; the revised text dropped it and does not name coal, oil or gas.
Negotiators from nearly 200 countries were divided over fossil fuels and climate finance.
Activists and some leaders criticized the draft, and environmental groups put pressure on host Turkey and lead negotiator Australia.

stories.headline: Britain and EU agree deals on food trade, carbon markets and youth mobility
stories.summary: Britain and the European Union agreed at a summit in Brussels on Friday to ease checks on food trade, cooperate on carbon emissions trading and set up a youth mobility scheme. An agreement on university tuition fees for EU students was put off. Prime Minister Andy Burnham called the package the limit of convergence during this Parliament, while a minister said rejoining the EU is "on the table" in the longer term, according to The Guardian.
stories.why_it_matters: For people in Britain and the EU, the deals could mean fewer border checks on food and new chances for young people to live and work across the Channel. They also reopen the debate over how close Britain should be to the EU.
stories.background: Britain voted to leave the European Union in 2016, a decade ago, and its exit added checks and paperwork to trade and ended free movement of people between the two. The two sides held a first summit in May 2025, where they agreed to work toward a deal on food and agricultural trade and a youth scheme. Andy Burnham, now prime minister, travelled to Brussels for Friday's summit, which produced a 12-page joint statement. The Wall Street Journal and others report that his government has started a debate about whether Britain should eventually rejoin.

facts.text: Britain and the EU agreed deals on food trade and youth mobility, according to a joint statement issued at Friday's summit in Brussels.
The agreements also cover emissions trading, according to The Guardian, The Hindu and France 24.
An agreement on university tuition fees for EU students in Britain was pushed back.
Burnham said the package was the "limit" of what the two sides would converge on during the current UK Parliament, which runs until 2029.
The two sides set out the agreements in a 12-page statement after months of negotiations, The Guardian reported.
The Guardian reported that Ed Miliband said rejoining the EU is "on the table".

stories.headline: Denmark expels Russian defence attaché over alleged plot to kill Ukrainian-American rapper
stories.summary: Denmark said on Friday that it had thwarted a plot by Russian intelligence to assassinate the rapper Kyivstoner at a concert near Copenhagen, and it ordered Russia's defence attaché to leave. The Russian embassy denied the allegation. Reuters reported that Denmark is now pressing other EU countries to tighten restrictions on Russians.
stories.why_it_matters: European governments say Russia is carrying out sabotage and attacks on their soil, and a plot against a performer at a public concert would put ordinary concert-goers at risk.
stories.background: Kyivstoner is the stage name of Albert Vasiliev, a rapper with Ukrainian and US citizenship. Danish officials say Russian intelligence services recruited members of a violent gang to kill him at a concert in Denmark scheduled for Sept. 25. Several European countries have accused Russia of sabotage and other covert operations on their territory since the invasion of Ukraine; this week Estonia said it would close its border with Russia after accusing Russian services of an attempted arson attack. Russia denies the accusations.

facts.text: Denmark said it thwarted a Russian plot to assassinate the US-Ukrainian rapper known as Kyivstoner.
Denmark's foreign minister said the Russian ambassador had been summoned and that Moscow's defence attaché in Copenhagen would be expelled.
Danish officials say Russian intelligence recruited members of a violent gang to carry out the killing at a concert outside Copenhagen, The New York Times reported.
The alleged target is Albert Vasiliev, and the concert was scheduled for Sept. 25, The Kyiv Independent reported.
Denmark also announced tighter restrictions, France 24 reported, and Reuters reported that a message to member states shows Denmark pushing the EU to tighten curbs on Russians.
European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen condemned the alleged plot and pledged solidarity with Denmark.

stories.headline: Haiti agrees prison-building deal with El Salvador as Salvadoran troops fight gangs
stories.summary: Haiti announced an agreement with El Salvador to build new prisons after a visit by a Haitian minister, the AP reported. El Salvador has sent at least 2,000 troops to Haiti to fight gangs, and President Nayib Bukele has launched a bid for a third term in February's election. Many Haitians have welcomed the troops, while human rights monitors have raised concerns.
stories.why_it_matters: Haitians have lived under gang control for years, and the deployment could bring some security, but El Salvador's methods have drawn criticism from rights monitors. The coverage in the digest comes from left-leaning and center outlets only.
stories.background: Armed gangs have controlled much of Haiti's capital, Port-au-Prince, for several years. Nayib Bukele, El Salvador's president, became known for a crackdown on gangs at home that included mass arrests and a large prison called Cecot. He has now deployed Salvadoran troops to Haiti, and Haiti's government approved a cooperation agreement with El Salvador this week. Axios reported in October that President Trump backed the deployment. Bukele is running for a third term in elections in February.

facts.text: Haiti announced an agreement with El Salvador for the construction of new prisons after a minister's visit.
Haiti's justice and public security minister visited El Salvador's Cecot prison on Tuesday, and Haiti's Council of Ministers approved a cooperation agreement with El Salvador.
Bukele said his troops attacked the home of a gang leader in Haiti, NBC News reported.
Bukele has formally launched a bid for a third term in February's elections; The Washington Post reported that it could keep him in power until 2033.
Many Haitians have welcomed the Salvadoran troops, while some fear the offensive could make a volatile situation worse, The Guardian reported.
Axios reported on Oct. 30 that Trump had approved of El Salvador's troop deployment to Haiti.

stories.headline: Phumzile Mlambo-Ngcuka, South Africa's first female deputy president, dies at 71
stories.summary: Phumzile Mlambo-Ngcuka, South Africa's first woman deputy president and a former head of UN Women, has died at 71, the South African government announced on Friday. Acting President Paul Mashatile, the UN secretary-general and the African Union Commission chairperson issued tributes.
stories.why_it_matters: She was one of the most senior women in South African politics and led the UN's agency for women's rights for eight years, shaping global work on gender equality.
stories.background: Mlambo-Ngcuka served as South Africa's deputy president from 2005 to 2008, the first woman to hold the post. She then led UN Women, the United Nations body for gender equality, as executive director from 2013 to 2021, with the rank of under-secretary-general. At the time of her death she was chancellor of the University of Johannesburg.
